Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Numerical examples highlighting the interconnection between model choice and predicted behavior have been provided, leading to a reflection on the responsibility of the computational mechanics community to consider the consequences of their simulations on the real world. Finally, a call to action is issued, encouraging researchers to develop more realistic numerical models that can accurately predict real-world phenomena and lead to innovations in science and technology. This work aims to stimulate a deeper conversation about the development of bond-based peridynamic models and their applications. This research was supported by NSF grant 1944594 and ONR grant N00014-19-23051. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. Researchers have studied this phenomenon in complex systems like insect colonies and fish, observing how noise can cause collective behaviors to emerge. In a new study, researchers investigated whether this phenomenon occurs in quantum systems as well, and found evidence of a new classically forbidden transition induced by quantum noise. They used a simple mathematical model of a system that can be studied analytically to explore how noise causes it to switch into a stable limit cycle state. What they found is that the noise-induced transition in the quantum system has properties that are fundamentally different from those found in classical systems, and that are also unique to quantum systems. These findings reveal a significant distinction between how noise behaves in quantum versus classical systems. Additionally, the researchers showed that this noise-induced transition in the quantum system can occur even if individual components are stable. You might expect that this requires a high level of disorder, but surprisingly, the amount of disorder required is actually lower in quantum systems than in classical ones. These discoveries provide first-time empirical evidence of a new classically forbidden transition induced by quantum noise and noise in general, and that quantum mechanics has unique ingredients that make it different from classical physics. It is also found that this noise-induced transition in the quantum system can occur through two distinct methods, and that these mechanisms are not present in classical systems. These

In this study, we demonstrate a more robust framework for identifying esophageal tumors by leveraging a diverse set of anomalous cases. Unlike existing methods that rely on classified tumors, we use a semi-supervised learning approach that takes advantage of both labeled and unlabeled scans to improve performance. , exploring alternative types of computer hardware can help mitigate the issues of slow communication between processing units and vast amounts of data. Two potential solutions, optical and nanoelectronic systems, have already led to the creation of successful hybrid devices that combine these technologies, such as field-programmable gate arrays. These hybrid systems, particularly those using the leaky nanowire FET, show great potential in neural network computations due to their low power consumption and high data storage capacity. Current hybrid optical-nanoelectronic networks, however, still rely on electronic switching, resulting in decreased overall efficiency. This paper envisions a future hybrid network that fully integrates optical signals for data transmission and nanoelectronic signals for data storage, and then demonstrates this concept through the development of a hybrid spin-orbit coupling-based photonic nanoelectronic neural network. This new hybrid system enables rapid, three-dimensional data transmission and storage at the nanometer scale, paving the way for high-speed, energy-efficient neural network computations. Additionally, by employing spin-based photons and CMOS-compatible nanoelectronic components, the latency and power requirements of hybrid optical-nanoelectronic networks can be substantially improved. Simulation results demonstrate that this new hybrid system can achieve significant reductions in latency and power consumption compared to existing hybrid systems. Furthermore, the study examines the practical implications of integrating SOCS-based photons and nanoelectronic components into a single hybrid device, and provides a roadmap for implementing this technology in neural network computing

By analyzing photometric redshifts, we examine the angular correlation of near-infrared selected galaxies in ten redshift bins and calculate their stellar mass distribution, which we compare to a model. We find that the mass of stars within a galaxy is directly proportional to the mass of its host halo and peaks at around $10^{12}\,M_{\odot}$. This is consistent with a scenario in which galaxies in more massive halos at higher redshifts have greater star-forming efficiencies. Furthermore, we determine that the fraction of satellite galaxies to central galaxies is lower at higher redshifts, but that satellites are predominantly less massive than centrals. We find that, in general, central galaxies have a higher contribution to the total stellar mass within a halo than satellite galaxies until halo masses exceed $10^{13}\,M_{\odot}$. This implies the presence of quenching mechanisms in large halos to limit star-forming activity. We compare these results to three hydrodynamic simulations, which generally overestimate the contribution of satellite galaxies to the total stellar mass within a halo, especially at high mass ends, indicating less efficient feedback in group-and cluster-scale halos or quenching occurring later. our research addresses a high-dimensional, sparsity-based linear regression challenge.
This problem involves numerous nodes connected to a central node, exchanging concise messages, 
each holding noisy samples of the same regression equation. 
The central node needs to accurately find and replicate the regression vector's support, 
under strict computation and communication limits. 
Our work explores a family of distributed algorithms based on Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, 
investigating their ability to find the regression vector's support in the given conditions. 
Our research reveals that these distributed algorithms are capable of exact support recovery 
under specific constraints, even at very low signal-to-noise ratios, where single devices can't identify 
the vector's support, at a communication cost linearly scalable. 
Our simulated data also demonstrates how these distributed OMP-based algorithms match the performance of 
more sophisticated methods in many instances, even outperforming them at times. 
Our simulations further highlight how these distributed algorithms handle missing data cases effectively. 
Our research also demonstrates that these distributed algorithms are capable of exact support recovery 
in various high-dimensional regression challenges, like the distributed vector pursuit problem and the distributed broadcast recovery problem. 
Our research explicitly shows that these distributed algorithms are capable of exact support recovery 
in the broadcast recovery problem under more relaxed conditions, leading to potential applications. 
Our research ultimately highlights the potential for these distributed algorithms to efficiently find 
the regression vector's support in various high-dimensional, distributed regression challenges.

Our research reveals that in the graph domain, GNNs utilizing recurrent aggregators perform equally well to existing permutation-invariant aggregators on synthetic and real-world problems. Despite their benefits, recurrent aggregators struggle to scale due to their $O(V)$ depth and difficulty in parallel processing large graphs. Motivated by the notion that an efficient aggregator should resemble a commutative monoid, we introduce a method for constructing trainable commutative and associative binary operators. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that while it cannot surpass the performance of recurrent aggregators, it offers a comparable level of performance while achieving significantly higher efficiency. Our work further proposes various instantiations of this new aggregator, leading to superior or comparable results to existing top-performing aggregators on multiple tasks. However, this approach faces challenges in achieving effective results as one task might negatively impact others, causing them to underperform. Despite current methods for loss balancing that depend on either complex optimization or detailed numerical analysis, our proposal involves directly scaling losses based on their observed magnitudes using various exponential moving averages techniques. Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question. To achieve accurate recognition, objects
that provide valuable context information should not be ignored in the
prediction process.
An alternative method called SCO for Receptive Field is proposed to make use
of the context information effectively. By pooling the feature maps of objects
that are within the receptive field of the target object, the context that is
potentially useful can be captured and integrated into the object detector.
It is observed that the context integration of SCO enhances the speed and
accuracy of the object detection application. A comparative analysis of how
different context integration methods function is conducted. The potential risks
of over-reliance on the context are also identified.

Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. In addition, the translation includes an updated version of Thomas Ramakrishnan and Roger Wilson's 1994 paper on the characterization of conjugacy classes in the symplectic group Sp_n(K). Ramakrishnan and Wilson built upon Springer's work, extending his results to fields K with a characteristic of two, while also incorporating additional forms (specifically, skew-hermitian and its relationship with hermitian forms). In this revised translation, the order of publication has been reversed to maintain consistency with the original research.

Variational quantum algorithms show great potential in near-term quantum simulation to outperform classical computers, particularly for simulating systems with complex interactions. We investigate these algorithms for their application in modeling the ground state of systems with extensive interaction and generating spin squeezed states. Our findings suggest that variational algorithms struggle with increased long-range interactions, leading to lower precision and more optimization steps required. However, we discovered that enhancing connectivity between distant qubits improves performance, utilizing fewer quantum and classical resources. Our results reveal that combining circuit layers with varying levels of connectivity can lead to enhanced outcomes, with layer order significantly influencing results, particularly when starting with layers facilitating long-distance connections. The circuit design can also be applied to variationally produce spin squeezed states, which serve as essential resources for quantum measurement accuracy. Our research provides crucial insights into the behavior of variational algorithms in simulating systems with extensive interactions and quantum measurement processes, ultimately facilitating the development of more efficient algorithm designs for near-term quantum simulators. Additionally, we provide open-source code allowing for the easy replication of our results. This code, along with related healthcare data simulation code, can be found on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/QAAYAN/vqos-inneartermquantumsimulators. , we have developed new techniques to estimate Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). A combined method of dimensionally decomposed generalized polynomial chaos expansion and Kriging (DD-GPCE-Kriging) is proposed, allowing for precise approximation of nonlinear random outputs. This DD-GPCE-Kriging method is integrated with Monte Carlo simulation and multifidelity importance sampling for enhanced performance. The Monte Carlo method efficiently uses the DD-GPCE-Kriging model to sample, however, it introduces bias due to the surrogate model. In response, we developed a multifidelity importance sampling approach where the DD-GPCE-Kriging method efficiently constructs a biasing density and the high-fidelity model is employed to calculate the CVaR using biased samples from the q-uniform distribution. Numerical tests demonstrate that this multifidelity approach is more accurate, especially for nonsmooth outputs, outperforming the standard Monte Carlo method. Furthermore, we demonstrate the scalability of the methods by successfully applying them to two complex engineering problems, including a 2D composite laminate and a 3D composite T-joint, both of which featured multiple partly dependent random inputs. The results reveal a 104x speedup for the multifidelity approach while accurately calculating the CVaR with minimal error. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. The proposed methods are made available through an open-source repository, enabling future research in this area. The experiments conducted provide valuable insights that can benefit the development of future incremental learning methods,

Capturing the cerebellar cortex's tightly foliated appearance is challenging due to its convoluted surface and the time-consuming process of manual segmentation. While human experts can contribute to segmentation quality, current automated labeling methods are limited by their susceptibility to errors. A new, 20 micrometer resolution dataset offers an enhanced platform for semantic segmentation compared to existing 1mm resolution magnetic resonance imaging. To bypass manual annotation requirements, we suggest training a model to automatically transfer annotated data from the Allen Brain Human Brain Atlas to the BigBrain dataset without supervision, accounting for staining and spacing variations. Deep learning-based methods have become the primary approach for object detection and many probabilistic object detection models have been developed recently. Unfortunately, a unified summary of uncertainty estimation in object detection has yet to be established due to the diverse architectures, uncertainty methods, and evaluation metrics used across existing models. Furthermore, different performance evaluation criteria are employed for various datasets, hindering the direct comparison and selection of a suitable model for a given application. This paper aims to bridge this gap by presenting an in-depth analysis and comprehensive comparison of existing probabilistic object detection methods designed for autonomous driving tasks. Initially, we cover fundamental uncertainty estimation concepts in deep learning before systematically surveying existing detection models and performance evaluation criteria. Subsequently, we introduce the AutOD dataset, a large dataset of object detection with varied uncertainty sources. Ultimately, we demonstrate the performance of 33 probabilistic object detection models on the AutOD dataset. Notably, this work is the first to thoroughly assess the dependency of detection performance on dataset size for autonomous driving tasks, revealing significant variations in performance up to moderate sizes. After that, we identify the top models and make our code, dataset, and model evaluations publicly available to facilitate future research in this domain. By promoting a deeper understanding of object detection uncertainty, we hope to advance autonomous driving applications and enable more robust incorporation of uncertainty estimation in future autonomous vehicle systems. This research is significant as it brings deep learning-based object detection one step closer to practical use in autonomous vehicles

an intriguing connection where increased educational attainment tends to exacerbate income disparity. The Mincer equation's nonlinear relationship between wages and education, along with the variability in its return on investment, appear to play crucial roles in this occurrence. A combined approach of least-squares and quantile regression analysis has been developed to disentangle these contributing factors. The new methodology relies on the functional derivative method and is subsequently applied to examine the case of Argentina from 1992 to 2015. Our findings indicate that the country's income inequality increased during this time period, largely due to a decrease in the average return to education as educational levels rose. In contrast, the wage growth rate across all levels of education exhibited a decline. Nevertheless, the overall increase in the return to education, measured using a weighted average based on the population's educational distribution, was hindered by the dominant influence of higher returns at the upper quantiles. In contrast, the behavior of the income growth rate across quantiles displays a U-shape, suggesting that both low and highly educated individuals experience similar income dynamics while those in the middle may see their incomes decline relative to educational investments. In comparison to previous studies on Argentina, our analysis yields two notable differences: (i) the country's income inequality evolved in a manner contrary to the 'paradox of progress,' and (ii) the observed U-shaped relationship between income growth rates and educational quantiles, rather than a sharp decline at intermediate levels, was evident. For achieving this goal, an innovative error estimator is presented, designed to overcome limitations of existing error estimation techniques that rely on the inf-sup constant in model order reduction. In the context of parametric problems, however, the inf-sup constant is inherently dependent on the parameters, resulting in inaccurate error estimates for certain scenarios where the constant is extremely low. A separate algorithm utilizing photometric data identified BHB candidates, which were then matched with the spectroscopic list to generate a database of 15,640 Blue Horizontal Branch stars spanning Galactocorticical distance. This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. By deriving precise analytical expressions for the mean and variance of local transmission delays in both protocols, and determining the optimal parameters that minimize these delays, this study proposes two distinct operating modes, correlation-limited and bandwidth-limited. Notably, while changing the frequency-hopping sequence length affects both the mean and variance of local delays, the impact of packet length is predominantly seen in the variance. a black hole is theoretically capable of growing unlimited, a concept denoted by the BSW effect. Traditionally, this effect assumes particles follow geodesic or electrogeodesic trajectories; in this version, a black hole is assumed static, and a single particle at rest is involved. When an incoming particle from an infinite distance collides with the stationary particle, the energy in the center of mass frame grows without bounds, illustrating the BSW effect. For nonextremal black holes, the necessary force to prevent such particles from escaping the event horizon increases indefinitely, whereas for an extremal horizon, this force remains finite and nonzero. For rotating black holes, neither the energy in the center of mass frame nor the force shows infinite growth, instead converging to a specific value. In cases involving an extremally charged black hole, the energy in the center of mass frame grows without bounds, provided that the charge on the stationary particle is sufficiently strong. When the charge on the stationary particle is zero or negative, the energy in the center of mass frame remains finite, and its value is closely related to the force required to prevent particles from escaping the event horizon, a value that remains finite and nonzero in such cases. In contrast to geometric properties, this effect appears to be related to the mass of the black hole itself, suggesting a fundamental connection between the influence of charge on the energy in the center of mass frame and the universality of the BSW effect. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's performance in this area. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interfering signals, we develop a mathematical model for calculating the outage probability of the ACN protocol and provide analytical expressions for the results. By comparing the ACN protocol to existing alternatives, we demonstrate that ACN yields a substantial improvement in outage probability at road intersections, particularly for higher data transfer rates. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations verify our theoretical findings. ## Step 1: Identify key components
The ACN protocol consists of two key components: $K$ and $m$.
$K$ represents the number of vehicles cooperating in relaying the message, and $m$ is the index of the vehicle selected for transmission.
## Step 2: Determine relevant parameters
The relevant parameters in this problem are the total number of vehicles $K$, the index of the vehicle selected for transmission $m$, the outage power $P_{out}$, the total interference power $I_{tot}$, and the bandwidth $B$.
## Step 3: Apply relevant theories
To calculate the outage probability of the ACN protocol, we utilize the Erlang formula combined with the law of large numbers to find the probability distribution of the interference power and its derived outcomes.

The emergence of memristive properties in transition metal oxides is generally attributed to the electromigration of oxygen vacancies at a nanoscale.  Focusing on Pt/TiOx/TaOy/Pt devices, our research investigates the transfer of oxygen vacancies between the device and its environment in response to electrical stress.  Through both experiments and theoretical simulations, we establish that the TiOx and TaOy layers exchange oxygen vacancies during the formation of nanoscale memristive bridges.  The simulations indicate that the electrostatic potential at the nanoscale enables the migration of oxygen vacancies through the material in response to current flow.  The results provide a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic behavior of oxygen vacancies within metal-oxide memristive devices.

In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing multiple beneficial tasks, and (2) minimizing random fluctuations in these tasks. In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. Here, these principles are extended to hybrid thermal machines with multiple terminals. In quantum conductors, these limitations are bypassed, and we demonstrate this for a setup comprising a double quantum dot and normal metals in contact, powered by an entangled Cooper pair generator. In this setup, it's possible to optimize the engine to produce maximum work by exploiting zero-energy states without increasing charge quanta randomness, or tuning the transmitter efficiency to minimize random fluctuations in charge quanta while capturing quantum states, or combining both for optimal performance. In contrast, conventional engines require a trade-off between efficiency and randomness. These novel strategies for quantum engineering open doors for cutting-edge nanotechnology and enable new generations of highly efficient nanodevices. In this study, it's also shown that it's possible to convert high entropy from the entangled Cooper pair generator into useful work by using multiple quantum states, thereby surpassing previous entropy conversion limits. The findings of this research are also extended to more complex systems, specifically Jordanian quantum eraser and the associated quantum thermodynamics, offering fresh perspectives on tunneling quantum states and work generation. This unmanageable amount of information poses significant challenges, making it nearly impossible for humans to comprehend the structure and nearly unfeasible for computers to process efficiently. In this context, text mining emerges as a burgeoning field, aiming to unlock valuable information within massive document repositories. Traditional machine learning methods, while powerful, are ill-equipped to handle the scale of text data, thereby necessitating more efficient and scalable approaches.

This dissertation presents a viable solution for addressing the text mining scalability issue by harmoniously integrating generative models with sparse computation techniques. A unified framework for text generative models is established, synthesizing previously distinct methods within this family, while also developing novel algorithms for clustering and topic modeling applications that leverage sparse computation for parameter estimation.

Our experimental evaluations across multiple text mining tasks demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed approach over established methods, particularly in uncovering meaningful categories and topics within large document collections. Furthermore, these experiments showcase the versatility of our proposed framework, as it successfully captures the structure of text data using a range of generative models. This dissertation further explores the general applicability of sparse computation in machine learning and data mining, highlighting its potential to address various challenges within massive data sets. Additionally, it sets forth future research directions for sparse computation in text mining and machine learning.

Another issue is that memristors have not yet developed into reliable and stable analog storage units for analog-weight synapses with gradual learning. Our study shows that we can build a monolithic chip core with pseudo-CMOL architecture that addresses these two technical problems. The core achieves density improvements by applying a geometrical chip layout technique that mimics CMOL architecture and by using a binary-weight learning rule for spike-timing-dependent plasticity. The learning rule utilizes the reliability of the binary storage capability of the used memristors. Our results demonstrate that we can construct a spiking neural network with approximately 8 million analog synapses on a chip

To tackle this issue, conventional methods typically involve aligning body part features according to external semantic cues or feature similarities, but this can be cumbersome and sensitive to noise. To address this challenge, our DRL-Net network learns a disentangled representation of person images without the need for pre-defined alignment or semantic cues. Through a dual transformation process, it decomposes the image into two components - a channel representing the semantic identity and a set of channels representing nuisance variables (occluded information). To minimize alignment issues, our local alignment loss (LAL) adjusts the occluded region by moving it to a closer location. deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges. Unfortunately, the conventional linear regression model is not equipped to handle these complexities. The emergence of new methods, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Multivariate Linear Regression (MLR), helps mitigate some of the issues, though they still cause bias. The introduction of Spurious Component Analysis (SCA), a novel method, successfully removes spurious logratios and their associated principal components. SCA identifies and eliminates noise in the data, resulting in improved model fit and accurate predictions. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the classic Sinkhorn-scaling algorithm is employed. Furthermore, a new model architecture based on the Bregman ADMM algorithm is designed, which offers better numerical stability and improved ability to reproduce existing pooling layers. The proposed UOTP layers are then tested across several applications, including multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification, and are found to be capable of either mimicking conventional global pooling layers or developing novel, performance-enhancing pooling mechanisms. Specifically, the integration of UOTP layers into a simple model yields superior performance on various image recognition datasets when compared to existing pooling layers. Our research, however, reveals that the Shapley Value systematically undervalues the contribution of a particular type of client, known as the Maverick. Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Furthermore, when integrated into a self-driving vehicle training pipeline, SceneGen is shown to provide a suitable approximation of actual traffic conditions. This study leverages mobile phone user movement data to show that, in Germany, mobility has not only been diminished, but the pandemic-induced lockdowns have also introduced lasting structural transformations to the nation's mobility network. Moreover, the pandemic-induced structural changes have been found to have a considerable effect on disease transmission dynamics by compressing the spread of epidemics and temporarily hindering the spread to remote regions. Consequently, these findings suggest that long-lasting epidemics may significantly alter a nation's mobility patterns, thereby affecting disease transmission dynamics and, in turn, the pandemic's course. The novel methods employed in this study provide new avenues for investigating the intricate interplay between human mobility, disease transmission, and pandemic propagation. The digital data traces of human mobility can be seen as a type of pandemic risk map, indicating the likelihood of disease transmission based on the structural properties of the mobility network. This study offers crucial insights for crafting effective control measures by combining digital data analysis with traditional epidemiological modeling, thereby providing policy makers with actionable strategies to mitigate pandemic spread. producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our method allows for low-loss optical communication. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the ability to control the flow of light through our system using a relatively weak control light, effectively allowing us to "switch on" and "switch off" the nonreciprocity. We were able to achieve this level of control while minimizing the power required, reducing it by at least two orders of magnitude compared to previous techniques. We believe this discovery will lead to the development of compact, low-power optical systems for communication and signal processing. Additionally, we've shown that our method can be used to build nonreciprocal optical clocks, enabling the reduction of systematic errors and allowing for the implementation of novel quantum measurement techniques. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. A collective behavior transition was found as model parameters were modified. The model exhibits two distinct regimes: a phase with coexistence and varied species distributions and a phase where one species dominates and displaces the other. The boundary between these phases is influenced by the intensity of random events. The model's behavior in the coexistence phase resembles a complex state known as "bistable chaos" observed in certain non-equilibrium many-body systems. A similarity was found between the model's species distribution and the distribution of energy levels in random matrix theory. A difference was noticed, however, in the species distribution's fluctuation pattern as compared to a standard noisy voter model. The model's behavior was further analyzed by evaluating its variability and observing the dominance of a few dominant species. The model's results were compared with experimental data from a study of two species of the bacterium Escherichia coli. The model's findings indicate that species competition often ends in the dominance of a single species due to random events interfering with colonization attempts. The model offers an approach for understanding species competition in biological systems and provides a framework for comparing theoretical predictions with biological observations. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance, however, struggles when dealing with failures that don't directly affect performance, leading to the development of RCanopus. RCanopus enhances Canopus to not only tolerate various types of failures but also to guarantee the accurate detection and recovery of failures and protect against malicious attacks, all while maintaining agreement among live nodes. Through the optimization of failure detection and recovery mechanisms, RCanopus reduces the overall system latency to detect and recover failures, limiting this delay to a constant O(log N) time. Moreover, RCanopus includes a voting system that prevents successful malicious attacks and protects the system from failure by requiring more than half of the live nodes to agree on any operation. As a result of combining these protections, RCanopus includes a linear recovery latency that limits the overall system latency to O(N) time in rare events. The inclusion of a membership management system also enables the accurate detection and recovery of more complex failures. Despite adding this management system, RCanopus maintains the same low failure detection latency as the original Canopus protocol. twisted trilayer graphene exhibits unique properties that have piqued researchers' interest. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be applied to existing data sets, significantly diminishing the attacker's yield. To overcome these drawbacks, we introduce an innovative adversarial attack, Adversarial Resampling, which enables an attacker to manipulate existing data sets, thereby skewing the model's predictions in their favor. Our results show that our attack, implemented as a black-box attack, can successfully deceive DNN models 70.9% of the time, an incidence nearly three times greater than existing MitM attacks. To mitigate this attack, we also propose an efficient detection method, utilizing an integral part of the attack, which achieves 75.9% accuracy in detecting adversarial samples. Our study may serve as a starting point for future research in defending against adversarial attacks in mobile applications. The source code for our approach is available at https://github.com/nader-alali/Adversarial-Resampling. We derive explicit expressions for key thermodynamic parameters, including the density of states, specific heat, susceptibility, and spin autocorrelation functions through semi-analytical calculations. These analytical results corroborate corresponding findings from Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, in the long-time autocorrelation function, we discover a decay pattern consisting of an inverse-time ($1/t$) damped harmonic oscillation under specific coupling conditions and develop a theoretical justification for this observation. We also show that in the high-temperature regime, a modified Arrhenius formula accurately predicts the autocorrelation function. Additionally, in the context of many-spin systems, we establish that the autocorrelation function of nearest-neighbor spins in the Heisenberg chain approximates that of the Maximal Causality model as the system size increases. This study provides a framework for analyzing and understanding the behavior of integrable models in the context of spin systems and their potential application in the future. Utilizing these findings, it may be feasible to devise a strategy for approximating the autocorrelation functions of nearly integrable systems as well. An integrable model like the one studied here could serve as a valuable benchmark for comparing the accuracy of simulation methods for evaluating autocorrelation functions. Implementing this model in experimental protocols might also aid in differentiating the characteristics of integrable and non-integrable systems through measurements of autocorrelation functions

This breakthrough is expected to open new doors for designing advanced quantum receivers. the Dirac field on a de Sitter space, considering its representation by two possible physical universes, reveals a distinction in significance between discrete isometries that preserve the structure and those that alter it, thus reducing the latter's importance. Focusing on the isometries of the expanding universe, which possesses a time-dependent scale factor, and ignoring those that apply only if the universe has a particular size, yields a set of discrete symmetries encompassing translations and rotations within a space with a hyperbolic structure. Applying these symmetries to the Dirac field leads to a classification of its unitary representations, which are unique and finite in number. Similarly, examining the Dirac field on a space of constant size, represented by its hyperbolic structure, yields a set of discrete symmetries encompassing translations and rotations, and a corresponding unique and finite number of unitary representations. In both cases, the discrete symmetries are found to be representable as finite-order Lie algebras. Here, the authors provide the first analysis of the discrete symmetries of the Dirac field on a de Sitter space, while also providing a new approach to understanding these symmetries and their relationship to the existing body of knowledge in the field. This work also offers a new, simple model for studying the properties of fermions in spaces of constant size, based on the principle of minimally coupling the Dirac field to the curvature of the space. burdensome due to the need for complete specifications. To mitigate this issue, gradual verification has been proposed, integrating static and dynamic checks to accommodate partial, complete, or absent specifications. Although it has been extended to cover recursive data structures on the heap, gradual verification has a significant drawback - users do not reap the benefit of decreased dynamic checks as specifications improve, and all properties continue to be dynamically validated regardless of any static guarantees. Moreover, a full-fledged gradual verifier does not yet exist, hindering the evaluation of its performance and applicability.

We developed Gradual C0, a practical gradual verifier for C0, a safe subset of C, specifically designed for educational purposes, to fill this gap. To optimize the insertion of dynamic checks and enhance efficiency, Gradual C0 relies on symbolic execution rather than backwards reasoning used in previous work. By overcoming technical hurdles associated with imprecise specifications, heap ownership, and branching in both program statements and specification formulas, Gradual C0 offers a viable solution. Moreover, we conducted an empirical performance evaluation and found that on average, Gradual C0 significantly decreases run-time overhead, averaging between 50-90% compared to a fully dynamic approach. The worst-case performance scenarios for Gradual C0 are predictable and preventable. This breakthrough enables the evaluation of gradual verification at scale. The system is freely accessible online. The dynamic checking system can be found at https://github.com/gradual-c0/gradual-c0 and the symbolic checker

Acting as selective barriers, membranes isolate cells due to the challenge ions face in traversing their dielectric shielding. In place of an outdated condition lacking dielectric properties, we introduce a new mathematical description that models a cell membrane with a lipid bilayer, embedded with channels allowing ions to pass selectively. This new framework, with a total of five variables, includes various physical properties such as membrane height, dielectric properties, and identified or unidentified ion distributions. To resolve ambiguities stemming from non-uniqueness, we focus on resolving dielectric properties and ion distributions using microscopic Poynting vector fields and macroscopic current measurements. Verifying the new description, we confirm its ability to reproduce known characteristics of cell membranes, ultimately providing a path to accurately characterizing unknown membranes at nanoscale resolution. This work has far-reaching implications for understanding biological processes, particularly ionic transport, and designing efficient energy-harvesting technologies that leverage dielectric energies. Its applications also extend to developing advanced materials making up tomorrow's dielectric interfaces between electronics and biology. In the future, we plan to utilize machine learning algorithms to optimize our new description and its various physical properties, enabling a wide range of nanoscale biological and physical investigations. Additionally, we aim to explore various other challenges, such as modeling DNA double helices and protein structures, to gain a deeper understanding of dielectric properties at the nanoscale. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary system's formation mass is influenced by its parent core's overall mass. In these simulations, they implemented azimuthally symmetric mass seeds within a rotating core, promoting the development of a dense filament, where a binary system might emerge. This binary formation process decreased as the core's mass increased, prompting researchers to amplify the core's kinetic energy ratio to its gravitational energy. This alteration led to increased binary mass and enabled a more precise prediction of a system's mass based on its parent core's mass. Furthermore, researchers created a graph to compare their results to actual proto-stellar masses, demonstrating that binary system formation tends to correspond to more massive core masses compared to single-star formation. Finally, researchers discussed the feasibility of performing a similar analysis for larger binary systems through the utilization of recent survey data, like the CZoom survey, focused on binary systems. This study aims to provide a foundation for future research on binary system formation, offering a pathway to differentiate between various formation processes. numerical approach to solve the time-fractional Black-Scholes equation. To tackle the issue of initial solution singularities, a time-adaptive finite difference method is proposed. This method utilizes the Alikhanov formula to approximate the fractional derivative, combined with the sum-of-exponentials technique, and an average spatial approximation for enhanced accuracy. By employing the energy method, the numerical scheme's stability and convergence are rigorously established with time second-order and space fourth-order accuracy. To validate the theoretical results, the numerical performance is demonstrated through several examples. Furthermore, the numerical solver developed based on this method is successfully utilized to price fractional barrier options, showcasing significant improvements over existing approaches. Specifically, for a given option, the time step size is determined by minimizing the absolute value of the inverse of the fractional derivative, and the spatial step size is chosen as the smallest value that yields a non-singular solution. Consequently, by using the proposed method, the time step size required to achieve a specified accuracy can be substantially reduced, thereby avoiding the'staircase' phenomenon prevalent in earlier fractional time-adaptive finite difference methods. Moreover, by enabling large spatial step sizes, the computational efficiency is enhanced for barrier options, whose Jacobian involves the derivative of the barrier function with respect to the underlying asset price. To further enhance the solver's efficiency, the storage of previously computed solution values is implemented. To confirm the superiority of the proposed approach, the computational time and numerical solutions obtained through this method are compared

Yet, the rapidly increasing complexity of scientific code coupled with the short lifespan of IT technologies poses significant obstacles to successfully recreating the data analysis environment, despite source code accessibility. There is a notable discrepancy between having version-controlled code and actually establishing an operational data analysis environment. We propose the creation of a snapshotting file system optimized for distributing software, which allows the preservation of varied data analysis environments. This is exemplified by our approach in replicating the data analysis software used to find the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach over conventional methods, such as package management, in preserving consistency throughout the software development lifecycle. Additionally, our approach enables simultaneous preservation of both human- and machine-accessible data, which expands the scope of software preservation beyond pure code. Ultimately, maintaining versions of data analysis environments using our snapshotting file system allows us to recall, or revive, historically significant software configurations, which is a novel application of this technique beyond its standard use in version management. In this context, we explore the implications of our approach for replicating scientific studies, as well as its potential for preserving software configurations in various other contexts. In contrast to replication, we focus on breaking down the problem into manageable software components and introducing a snapshotting file system to seamlessly recreate complex data analysis environments. Furthermore, we advocate for integrating our approach with existing package management systems to create a user-friendly data analysis

The primary issue lies in current travel demand modeling methods, which often generate overly optimistic and unrealistic trips that fail to reflect actual passenger choices. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of "mini activities" - short tasks that travelers perform during their journeys - to explain the divergence between simulated and observed trips. By utilizing data from smart cards, we can uncover these mini activities and incorporate them into the simulated trips. Furthermore, we've developed an approach that learns how to seamlessly integrate these mini activities into the simulated trips by leveraging both historical trip data and trip planner recommendations. By applying this approach, we can build a more accurate Markov chain for trip simulations, which effectively minimizes discrepancies between planned and observed trips. Experimental results obtained from testing on a dataset of passenger trips in Nancy, France, demonstrate substantial improvements in reducing these discrepancies. These improvements also enable more realistic simulations, which can, in turn, enhance the effectiveness of service evaluations and supply adaptations. To facilitate reproducibility, we've made our source code and demonstration materials publicly available online. By extending the boundaries of current travel demand modeling methodologies, this research aims to contribute to more realistic and informative trip simulations that can inform public transportation service provisioning and supply decisions. momentum distribution of electron-positron pairs was analyzed using the quantum kinetic equation, focusing on the distinct characteristics of Gaussian and Sauter pulse envelopes. Despite their similarity in temporal structure, the two pulse types yield a positron spectrum with a sharp peak adjacent to an essentially unaltered quantum induction current, a phenomenon absent in pulse shadows. The peak's amplitude shows an anisotropic dependence on the pulse envelope. For a Sauter pulse, the peak's magnitude increases significantly as the pulse amplitude approaches its critical value, resulting in a highly anisotropic spectrum with a positron momentum distribution that is much more pronounced than its electron counterpart. In contrast, for a Gaussian pulse, the peak's magnitude does not exhibit such a substantial increase, and it remains relatively independent of the pulse amplitude for values below its critical value. In all cases, the electron spectrum remains relatively unchanged from its quantum induction current value. The analysis also demonstrates that the positron spectrum becomes highly anisotropic when the pulse amplitude is close to its critical value, whereas it remains relatively isotropic for values below this threshold. In addition, the impact of pulse chirping on the momentum distribution was examined, revealing that varying the pulse duration causes changes in both the positron and electron spectra. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the space of generated sentences in natural language is dominated by a few dense retrieval samples, leading to the conclusion that dense retrieval plays a crucial role in uncovering fundamental language patterns. Ultimately, our research showcases the potential for substantial improvements in state-of-the-art models through simple, effective methods like ReCross. A specific focus is placed on the dynamic causal Bayesian optimisation (DCBO) method. We contend that by utilising a simulated network view and a causal model representing how an adversary propagates through the network, DCBO can function as a counter-agent. The primary goal of our study is to investigate DCBO's ability to identify and execute optimal interventions on host nodes to reduce the costs associated with security breaches caused by the adversary. The study showcases a comprehensive cyber simulation system which we employ to collect observational data for DCBO and presents numerical findings as a stepping stone towards future research in this domain. Notably, we observe that DCBO can yield multiple optimal intervention start times that yield the same overall optimal outcome, thereby necessitating the examination of intervention durations in addition to timing. We introduce a novel optimisation problem called the integrated optimisation problem, and propose a practical solution by transforming it into a more manageable mixed-integer linear programming problem. The study also presents various alternative scenarios where DCBO is informed by diverse simulated network views and adversary models, and reveals that DCBO can exhibit sub-optimal performance when using poor models. In addition, we outline practical procedures for translating DCBO's optimal interventions into tangible mitigation strategies on network hosts. This research provides basic causal models and simulation frameworks that can be expanded upon to capture real-world complexities in order to increase the practical applicability of DCBO.

First-principles computations and theoretical models indicate that CaTe
exhibits node-line semimetal characteristics under the exclusion of spin-orbit
interactions, with an accompanying drumhead-shaped surface state. When
spin-orbit interactions are incorporated, the node lines transform into a
pair of Dirac points along the M-R axis. This Dirac points structure is stable
due to the influence of C4 rotational symmetry. The presence of C4 symmetry
is necessary for maintaining the Dirac points; if this symmetry is disrupted,
the system converts into a topologically insulating state. The conversion is
reflected in changes to the surface state morphology and electronic properties
near the Dirac points. The node-line to Dirac points transition in CaTe offers a
rare opportunity to study topological semimetal transitions via experimental
and theoretical analysis. The insulating state emergence upon symmetry disruption
makes CaTe an appealing system for exploring topological transition phenomena. 
Additionally, the C4 ring of Fermi arcs in CaTe sets it apart from other Dirac
semimetals. The predictions made in this study can be validated through various
experimental techniques, including photoemission spectroscopy and
transport measurements. Furthermore, the predictions of this study can be
extended to other potential node-line semimetals, such as SrTe, MgQSi2, and
MgHGe, by evaluating their sensitivity to spin-orbit interactions.

Typically, prior object knowledge is incorporated by aligning a pre-established 3D model with the 2D image. To obtain more manageable approximate solutions, practitioners often employ a range of local search methods. Despite their extensive use, selecting the most suitable variant for a given problem remains a daunting task even for seasoned experts.

This paper breaks down local search algorithms into three distinct algorithmic elements, framing their sequential application within an optimization process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). By designing a deep graph neural network as a policy model for this MDP, the authors create NeuroLS, a learned controller for local search that surpasses existing controllers in operations research as well as more recent machine learning-based approaches, backed by a substantial body of experimental evidence. Furthermore, the researchers successfully integrate NeuroLS into a real-world scheduling problem of rail transport, demonstrating its efficacy in practice. Additionally, the authors propose a novel method using in-distribution sampling to transfer knowledge from larger to smaller problems within the same distribution, enhancing the scalability of their approach. Notably, NeuroLS achieves improved solution quality over current state-of-the-art local search methods while reducing computation time by a factor of 3 to 4 in tested problem instances. On a related learning-to-search problem, the authors observe a notable transfer effect from smaller to larger problem sizes within the same distribution and demonstrate a method to achieve this transfer using in-distribution sampling. unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning was the best that could be anticipated.   - Common Distribution Assumption: We introduced a common distribution assumption, common to both sender and adversary, which facilitates the construction of both public-key and private-key unclonable encryption schemes with multiple uses, founded on minimal assumptions. Our research also explores the public-key setting under another common distribution assumption, resulting in a construction with multiple uses, though it no longer meets the tightness limit of $0.5^n$ for cloning advantage.

Causality's applications extend beyond traditional fields such as epidemiology and the social sciences to the critical evaluation of the fairness of automated decision-making processes, both legally and in real-life situations. We examine the arguments and examples illustrating the importance of causality in ensuring fairness and identify the social consequences of non-causal predictions, highlighting the reliance of the legal system on causal evidence to prevent discrimination. We discuss the practical limitations and challenges of incorporating causality and offer potential solutions. Finally, we propose a research agenda to integrate the causal reasoning framework with machine learning and the social sciences to create a more transparent and fair automation of decision-making processes. This study is a call to action for researchers from diverse domains, including philosophy, statistics, law, and computer science, to collaborate in developing a more just and fair future, both on and off the internet. We hope this research will lead to a more open and honest relationship between the social sciences and the computer science community. We believe that successful automation of decision-making processes relies on a common, open-source and interpretable code that incorporates the principles of causal reasoning, is maintained jointly by philosophers and computer scientists, and is certified in court

To reduce data storage demands and overcome limitations in computational power, a new class of efficient lossy data compressors has been utilized in workflow processes, enabling the storage of detailed post-analysis data. In this research paper, we introduce an innovative adaptive approach that dynamically configures lossy data compression for various simulation components using sophisticated quality assessment algorithms. This contribution is multi-faceted: Firstly, we develop a novel method to identify optimal error limits for each simulation partition by replicating the entropy estimation process of a renowned lossy compressor, enabling informed lossy compression configurations. Secondly, we establish predictive models to estimate the overall data loss caused by lossy compression and calculate compression ratios based on specific partition properties. Thirdly, we develop a streamlined optimization strategy to identify the optimal combination of lossy compression configurations for various partitions, ensuring efficient resource allocation. Fourthly, we experimentally validate our methods on a parallel dataset of 768 entities, demonstrating the efficacy of our adaptive approach over fixed schemes. Ultimately, we integrate our techniques into the prefix sum tree-based partitioning algorithm, enabling scalable and efficient application of our methods to diverse datasets. In addition, we apply our methods to secondary memory scenarios, enabling the determination of optimal error limits for primary and secondary memory partitions. This research contributes high-quality algorithms for efficient data analysis, enabling the storage of detailed post-analysis data with minimal data loss. Furthermore, these methods facilitate scalable lossy compression configurations for diverse datasets, enabling fundamental applications in scientific computing

Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the graph's pathwidth, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the graph's branch number. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but leave room for improvement in dealing with non-stationary and dynamic environments. In contrast to previous works that rely on pre-defined observation spaces, $F^{2}I L$ employs end-effector pixel features through a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to observe the environment and learn an action model through a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The verification of formally designed abstract interpreters is a sophisticated endeavor, requiring considerable expertise in proof assistants and interactive evidence. This study introduces a fully formalized and proven abstract interpreter constructed using the F* verification framework. The incorporation of F* refinement types and SMT proof tools facilitates significant reductions in verification efforts compared to previous, interactive approaches. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies, making wrapper approaches impractical. Furthermore, wrapper methods focus on predicting a specific disease or phenotype, neglecting the broader temporal structure of the sequence. To address these limitations, we propose the Time-PCA method, which utilizes Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to simultaneously reduce dimensionality, retain temporal characteristics, and detect significant variables. Time-PCA defines sample similarity using a weighted Gaussian kernel based on the profile's temporal structure and performs PCA on the resulting matrix to identify principal components. These components are then used in a predictive model, such as a logistic regression, to predict disease or phenotype predictions. To evaluate the effectiveness of Time-PCA, we applied our method to multiple datasets, comparing its performance to other dimensionality reduction techniques and the wrapper approach provided by the R package 'elemSeq'. Our results demonstrate that Time-PCA outperforms the alternative approaches, retaining crucial variables with strong temporal structures that contribute significantly to the predictive model's accuracy. Additionally, the Time-PCA package includes the 'pcakmeans' cluster method, enabling the detection of underlying patterns in unseen data by utilizing the retained variables. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing bidding range of both a first-price auction and a sealed bid auction. To explain this, our theory suggests that some bidders treat uncredible auctions as a form of bidding war, limiting their bids to maintain prospects for future auctions. In contrast, auctions known to be run honestly encourage more aggressive bidding. Interestingly, bids in an uncredible second-price auction are slightly more aggressive than in a first-price auction, despite the latter often being perceived as honest. These findings have significant implications for real-world auctions where the credibility problem can arise due to tied auction runners or multiple auction platforms competing in a single auction. In such cases, bidding tactics may be influenced more strongly by the awareness of potential auction malfeasance than previously thought. This new understanding can aid auction designers in designing more effective bidding strategies, particularly when attempting to elicit a desired allocation by running an auction. In addition, the findings may prompt reevaluation of the approach taken by regulatory bodies, such as the Federal Communications Commission, which relies heavily on the premise that bidding tactics in auctions are solely driven by private valuations. In contrast, this study reveals the potential for a public strategy to outperform a private one in various auction scenarios. In a separate examination

Continual learning for semantic segmentation, a developing area, aims to upgrade an existing model by adding new categories step by step. Typically, the process of DTL begins by initially training DNNs on general knowledge and then utilizing them for specific tasks through a refinement process called fine-tuning. There have been two commonly observed patterns of transferability among pre-trained DNNs: one being that larger gaps between pre-training data and downstream information result in lower transferability and another indicating that transferability tends to decline from the initial to the final stages of DNNs. Nevertheless, these findings were primarily based on natural image datasets, thereby restricting their scope. This work endeavors to expand our understanding and build upon these findings by developing a method to measure the transferability of pre-trained DNN parameters across diverse datasets. Experimental findings conducted on twelve distinct image classification datasets corroborated existing theories but, more crucially, also revealed two additional insights, namely: one being that larger datasets and heightened data variety for the target task can also hinder transferability and two being that even though initial stages of DNNs may pick up fundamental image characteristics, these stages tend to be more susceptible to domain-specific factors. Consequently, knowledge is often not effectively transferred and instead gets corrupted in later stages during fine-tuning. We delve into cutting-edge Hebrew NLP by investigating applications of style transfer, using a recent model based on the GCLIP style transfer framework. This model utilizes a conditional variation of the Neumann neural encoder to effectively apply style transfer between two complex languages, enabling the transfer of styles from one language to another while preserving the original sentence structure. Demonstrating the effectiveness of this model, we successfully implement style transfer between Hebrew and English, achieving this difficult task despite Hebrew's distinctive characteristics. Additionally, we showcase the potential of this model by using it to create natural-sounding Hebrew sentences based on their counterparts in English. The outstanding performance of this model is a testament to the power of recent neural methods in NLP. Moreover, by achieving style transfer between languages with significantly different levels of morphological complexity, we believe we have set an important benchmark for future NLP models. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings from a theoretical perspective, highlighting potential future areas of research. By examining the issues that our model encounters during style transfer, we think we have identified some important limitations that could be addressed in the near future by NLP developers. This study provides the first thorough examination of style transfer between languages with highly disparate levels of morphological complexity

We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. Ultimately, this work seeks to provide a clear understanding of the evolution of spatial structures within diffusion populations. We demonstrate that although temporal diffusion characteristics appear stable and uniform, they yield diverse and ever-changing spatial structures that can be accurately captured through a straightforward generalization of established methods. We explore the applications of this approach to predicting population counts and estimating model parameters in both simulated and real-world datasets. Our analysis reveals that it can effectively identify key process features, even in cases where underlying assumptions are violated. Moreover, we show that it can accurately estimate key parameters in a wide range of diffusion processes, such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants, even when sample sizes are relatively small. As a result, this method is versatile and easy to understand, making it a great alternative to more complex methods, especially given its ease of use and small sample size requirements. Enhancing EURs' lower bounds can improve predictions of measurement outcomes and increase the reliability of quantum information processing.
To address this need, EURs for multiple, interconnected observables in complex systems have not been adequately established yet.

The process of business process simulation begins with a business process model annotated with simulation parameters, known as a business process simulation model. Research has proposed automated methods to discover business process simulation models from event logs extracted from enterprise information systems, utilizing process mining techniques. These approaches calculate activity processing times based on event log start and end timestamps. Nevertheless, the actual start times recorded in the event logs may not always accurately reflect when the activities commenced, often due to discrepancies in when the activities started and when the related data was logged. For instance, a resource may begin working on an activity but the actual start time is logged at a later point in time, after they interact with the system. Failing to account for such delays introduces inaccurate waiting periods, where a resource is logged as available, even though they are actively working. To overcome this limitation, a proposed method will determine and correct the waiting periods prior to each activity, ensuring their recorded start times accurately reflect actual processing times. The approach is founded on the notion that an activity can commence as soon as it is enabled, with its corresponding resource being available, hence it aims to estimate the activity enablement and resource availability times and correct the activity start times accordingly, reflecting the unrecorded processing times. The approach is tested on eight real-world event logs and is shown to accurately capture the activity start times at or close to the actual times

Yet, assigning responsibility for an ad impression to the right webpage becomes a difficult task in real-world scenarios, given the intricate scale and variability of advertising distribution systems. In this study, a novel type of deception is introduced, known as placement laundering, which targets weaknesses in the ad attribution mechanisms. Through placement laundering, malicious actors manipulate the ad display system, resulting in artificially inflated revenue generated by fake high-quality publisher origins. We elaborate on placement laundering, illustrate two instances found in practice and discuss one of these cases which involves abusing the intended features of the commonly used SafeFrame environment. Furthermore, a placement laundering detection system capable of identifying common forms of this type of deception is introduced along with experimental results of this method. A comparison of different solutions for protecting ads against placement laundering is also conducted. A placement laundering attack is successfully carried out using a malicious domain within the CPM model of the AdSense network and yields substantial profits, thereby demonstrating the severity of this type of deception. Additionally, a placement laundering detection system is introduced that employs SafeFrame API calls and can accurately identify over 90% of placement laundering transactions in test cases despite not exploiting any vulnerabilities in the ad display environment. A comparison of different methods for protecting ads against placement laundering is conducted, revealing that relying solely on IP blocking or whitelisting does not adequately safeguard against this type of deception as it fails to prevent over 90% of placement laundering transactions in test cases.
