Unfortunately, accurately predicting the duration a program may run, or even whether it will stop, is generally infeasible.
As a result, modern analysis tools typically focus on specific operations and rely on several simplifying assumptions.
Precisely identifying these constraints and critical program regions generally necessitates access to source code, specialized tools, and domain expertise.
Modifying even a single instruction often forces a repeat of this complex process, which becomes extremely time-consuming during iterative code development for performance-critical software.
We introduce MCAD, a new lightweight framework for analyzing the effects of code modifications at the microarchitectural level in binary programs, providing fast and accurate predictions of throughput changes.
MCAD employs a combination of whole-program emulation and instruction-level analysis, facilitated by common tools, allowing developers to identify critical execution paths rapidly with minimal overhead.
To our knowledge, MCAD uniquely addresses the challenge of rapid turnaround times for throughput estimation by orders of magnitude, outperforming current best tools.
A detailed assessment reveals MCAD to effectively scale for large programs with millions of instructions like FFmpeg and Clang, yielding < 3% average error in throughput estimation compared to hardware measurements.

Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
Our approach utilizes McGough's fog detection network and enhances it by adding a discriminative layer to produce probabilities for all three weather types from the three separate outputs of the pre-trained model.

By applying this framework to SARS-CoV-2, which caused the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers discovered evidence of self-organized critical dynamics, characterized by avalanche behavior, scaling relations, and slow auto-correlation decay. The experiment used sealed water phantoms, created through 3D printing, that were exposed to X-rays, protons, and carbon ions at varying intensities up to 340 Gy per second. Oxygen levels were measured using an optical sensor that enabled non-invasive detection. The results revealed that oxygen consumption is solely dependent on the radiation's dose, rate, and energy transfer. Oxygen levels decreased by 0.04-0.18 percent per 10 Gy for 225-kV X-rays, 0.04-0.25 percent per 10 Gy for 224 MeV protons, and 0.09-0.17 percent per 10 Gy for carbon ions. Oxygen consumption slowed as the radiation intensity increased, due to the self-interactions of radicals at higher dose rates, resulting in reduced oxygen consumption at these higher rates. The researchers also found that clinical doses did not completely deplete oxygen levels, even at 10 Gy dose delivery. Ultimately, the study concluded that Flash radiation does deplete oxygen but not to the point of total depletion, with higher dose rates actually resulting in lower oxygen consumption than standard radiotherapy rates. The researchers also discovered that the type of radiation used does not significantly affect oxygen consumption. The study provides essential insights for clinical trials of Flash radiation, which will reach unprecedented dose levels in human patients. ayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersions at two Fermi points when high-order contributions are disregarded, differs qualitatively from that of single-layer graphene. We found that this difference leads to short-range interactions that are marginally relevant. Through the use of the renormalization group to investigate these interactions' effects on the system's properties, it was observed that, at zero temperature, the two quadratic Fermi points would spontaneously divide into four Dirac points, giving rise to a nematic state with lattice symmetry breaking. In this nematic state, the system's six-fold lattice rotation symmetry, along with its layer permutation, decreases to a two-fold rotation, accompanied by a particular type of structural distortion where the two layers twist relative to each other. Moreover, this type of distortion gives the nematic state its distinctive identity. In addition to this behavior, it was also noticed that, at a finite temperature, the system would exhibit a unique type of phase transition, referred to as a thermal nematic phase transition, that results from the renormalization of its quadratic Fermi level behavior to linearly dispersive, resulting in the spontaneous breaking of its lattice rotation symmetry at a temperature consistent with the system's Kondo coupling constant multiplied by the system's bandwidth. In this type of transition, it was also seen that the system's layer permutation symmetry is preserved. Furthermore, it was pointed out that this type of nematic state with lattice symmetry breaking may also be induced by a significant applied electric field

, called Transfer Entropy, attempts to quantify information exchange between two signals by ignoring a target signal's self-predictive qualities. Transfer Entropy, however, often fails when dealing with signals like narrowband signals which exhibit self-predictability and are frequently observed in brain activity. A study demonstrated the inadequacy of traditional Transfer Entropy approaches by showing their failure to accurately measure narrowband signal relationships. A new approach is suggested, which first removes self-prediction patterns in signals by "whitening" them before evaluating their directionally-dependent time-based connections. This improved method resolves the issues encountered in simulated narrowband signal tests. The results show a more reactive role of the delta band and stronger involvement of the theta band in brain processing of the stimuli, which may provide further insights into frequency-dependent brain connections. The improved method could serve as a valuable tool in analyzing targeted frequency bands within complex biological systems. Using colloidal hard-sphere fluid experiments that necessarily come into contact with sample cell walls where non-uniform crystallization may occur, our work focuses on the simulation-based investigation of homogeneous versus heterogeneous crystallization. This study presents simulation results on the influence of different confining walls on the nucleation process, combining these findings with earlier data on homogeneous nucleation. Based on these results, the balance between homogeneous and heterogeneous nucleation can be determined depending on the wall type, fluid density, and system size. Walls coated with spheres have been found to overwhelmingly induce heterogeneous crystallization. Nonetheless, surfaces coated with spheres that are approximately three times the diameter of the fluid spheres - used in previous experiments - result in a likely dominance of heterogeneous crystallization below a 0.535 volume fraction. Only when walls mimic the fluid's disorderly structure does homogeneous nucleation appear more probable. These disordered coatings hold potential in minimizing wall-induced heterogeneous crystallization in experiments. Furthermore, the simulation reveals that homogeneous nucleation rates taking into consideration crystallite formation in both the bulk and at walls match rates from experiments classified as "homogeneous nucleation." This finding implies that heterogeneous crystallization could explain significant discrepancies between experimental measurements and simulations of homogeneous nucleation rates. To validate this assertion, the overlap between measured and simulated nucleation rates on various surfaces needs to be examined. This examination could provide concrete evidence that heterogeneous crystallization is more prominent than previously thought. Providing additional insight

Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. A range of innovative methods have been developed in an attempt to surpass supervised alternatives. A significant challenge in SSL lies in ensuring that its approaches remain robust across different environments. This paper marks a first in acknowledging that SSL has inherent limitations arising from its reliance on a single guiding principle. To overcome these limitations, we have leveraged uncertainty representation to create a more robust and universally applicable hierarchical training protocol that is compatible with any existing SSL model. This improved approach is based on a fundamental concept called the information bottleneck principle and decomposes the feature learning process into two distinct training phases with separate supervision mechanisms. This dual-supervision strategy encompasses two pivotal steps: 1) data augmentation invariance and 2) fuzzy pseudo-labeling that incorporates both hard and soft annotation inputs. This novel protocol allows for learning shared features across multiple classes and categories and achieves its goal through a combination of data augmentation invariance and pseudo-labeling of original samples during a two-phase training process. We examine several alternative scenarios involving double supervision and evaluate our method's efficacy on recent models representing four different self-supervised learning paradigms: geometrical, contrastive, non-contrastive, and hard/soft redundancy reduction. A range of experiments demonstrate that our training protocol enhances the performance of existing models without regard to their distinct underlying theories. Moreover, our method's performance is comparable to that of its hard-supervision counterparts. We also discovered

This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-hard. A detailed analysis of the properties of strong geodetic subsets is provided, along with an examination of the parameters that influence the size of a strong geodetic subset. Furthermore, a framework for unique path coverage in graphs is introduced, along with the development of efficient algorithms to tackle this challenge. Finally, a set of strong geodetic subsets is identified, which can be achieved by completing cycles in certain graphs, which also demonstrates the feasibility of designing exact algorithms for special types of graphs. Additional exact algorithms are developed for chords, cacti, and pseudotorus graphs. Medical dataset annotation for use in training data-hungry deep learning models is costly and time-consuming. Leveraging information from clinical practices, such as medical records or measurements, can greatly reduce these costs. However, precise lesion identification using automated processes is complex. We propose an enhanced loss function to focus the training on critical identification stages. By cross-training our cleaned model with these stages, we were able to greatly reduce detection latency by over 5.9 times while maintaining high accuracy at 94.2%. The findings support the importance of noise reduction in deep learning training for further enhancing model efficiency. The cleaned model, as well as the training code, have been made publicly available. The public release includes the cleaned dataset, training code, and corresponding model. Our approach can be applied to any dataset with associated clinical information to remove noisy data and thereby improve deep learning model training.

However, there is a notable lack of up-to-date tools capable of supporting such an innovative methodology. In response to this need, the authors of this paper propose a new verification tool called ChiselVerify.  ChiselVerify is an open-source tool for checking the integrity of electronic circuits designed with the help of any hardware design language.  ChiselVerify is built on top of Chisel, utilizing Scala and the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) for testing and verification purposes.  ChiselVerify is centered around three key concepts.  Firstly, the tool is designed to enhance the productivity of verification engineers by facilitating hardware testing within modern, high-level programming environments.  Secondly, the versatility of Chisel allows the tool to work seamlessly with a wide range of hardware design languages.  Thirdly, the tool is closely integrated with the existing Chisel universe, serving as a complementary extension of current testing libraries.  ChiselVerify's design was inspired by SystemVerilog functionalities, providing verification engineers with a wide range of testing capabilities such as functional coverage, constrained-random verification, bus functional modeling, and more within the high-level programming paradigm. The objective is to contribute to the ongoing development of efficient and effective models for automated essay grading and related applications in Natural Language Processing

This research presents a new, data-driven method for measuring skin tone in images, allowing accurate representations of skin tone using a single image without requiring consistent lighting or a standard background. The proposed method uses the dichromatic reflection model to break down skin regions into diffuse and specular components in RGB space. By analyzing the Specular Diffuse combination, four dimensions of skin tone can be represented, and the results show that this method accurately models skin tone across different lighting conditions and demographic groups without relying on labeled data or a single reference point. The proposed method's ability to represent skin tone in any situation, its ease of use, and its ability to model complex scenes make it a valuable tool for researchers studying demographic disparities in face recognition. The code for the method is available at https://github.com/IndigoPhoton/SkinToneAnalysis. The dataset used in the research is available at https://nextyy.nextlab.org/. , involves eliminating statistical redundancy from data to achieve more efficient storage. However, traditional data compression relies on prior knowledge of the data distribution. To overcome this limitation, a new approach called reverse compression has been developed. Reverse compression method applies universally to both classical and quantum information processes, relying solely on the channel to be used. All input data leading to indistinguishable outputs are compressed to a single state, regardless of their prior distribution. Furthermore, reverse compression can be viewed as a higher order preprocessing operation. We examine its applicability to erasure channels, revealing that while noiseless reverse compression may only occur in isometric channels, efficient reverse compression is possible in more general channels, including those that incorporate memory. Additionally, the principle of reverse compression has potential applications in the development of preprocessing techniques for quantum channels. To illustrate this, we identify a specific type of channel for which reverse compression can be effectively utilized. We further propose that reverse compression may provide insights into developing effective preprocessing methods for quantum channels. To test this, we explore its application to the amplitude damping channel. We discovered that while reverse compression may not always yield maximum entropy output for all input states, it can, however, be used to calculate the maximum entropy output for specific input states. We developed an iterative method to determine the optimal reverse compression operator and examined its behavior for various input states in the isotropic amplitude damping channel. The randomness inherent in turbulence and wave conditions makes the resulting loads more accurately described as probabilistic events rather than fixed values. The effect of these stochastic factors on the loads is more significant than the variability in the turbulence, and thus heteroscedasticity is present. Existing methods for adjusting a robot's trajectory or impedance have focused on specific uncertainties, such as detecting human intentions or uncertainty-based learning from demonstration. These approaches fall short in addressing multiple uncertainties that commonly occur in tasks. This study introduces a more comprehensive framework to improve adaptability - using model predictive control (MPC) to simultaneously plan a robot's trajectory and impedance. This MPC method can address various uncertainties, prioritize safety constraints, and be applied efficiently across tasks. Key sources of uncertainty considered include variable contact constraints, shifting human goals, or unforeseen disturbances. To develop an adaptable task model, Gaussian Processes are used to analyze a few demonstrations (up to three). This model then informs an optimization problem resolved by MPC, incorporating safety constraints and temporary human goal estimates to ensure secure and successful task execution. This MPC-based method is shown to improve performance across multiple uncertainties, compared to using a fixed trajectory or impedance. Additionally, it prioritizes safety throughout the adaptation process. This approach has been validated through two experiments - one involving a cooperative task and the other a corrective action - where a humanoid robot successfully incorporated various adaptations to overcome multiple uncertainties, successfully planning both its trajectory and impedance. This method allows a robot to efficiently handle and learn from multiple uncertainties, prioritizing safety and adaptive task execution. in virtually prototyping autonomous robots. We introduce a novel camera model validation method that compares real and simulated images through features extracted from pixel data, opposed to traditional geometric or photometric approaches that rely on ground truth. This method enables the assessment of a robot's vision system on actual hardware, prior to physical deployment. By integrating this evaluation into the simulation loop, we can identify and address issues in the simulation, ultimately refining both the simulation model and the robot's software before initiation. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in virtually prototyping an autonomous navigation system for a drone, employing a real dataset to train a deep learning-based classifier in the simulated environment. This demonstrates the feasibility of using simulated visuals to guide the development of autonomous robots, from high-level strategies to low-level control mechanisms. Additionally, we provide access to our simulation framework, which combines the SunCG simulator with the PyTorch deep learning library, facilitating the adoption of simulated camera features. This framework, along with our model validation approach and autonomous navigation system, are made available for public use at the provided links. By promoting the open-source replication of our methods, we aim to contribute to the advancement of autonomous robot development. Ultimately, this contribution aims to demonstrate the value of simulated camera features in autonomous robot development, from simulation to real-life deployment, and explore their applications in various computer vision tasks. Moreover, it highlights the benefits of virtually prototyping autonomous robots, enabling the precise calibration of ground truth and facilitating the transition to real-world settings

This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
Moreover, the proposed approach requires significantly less data than the methods
it compares to and can be applied to estimating queue lengths in various scenarios
without additional information. The method's performance is consistent across different
intersection types and environments, as validated by a sensitivity analysis. The
results indicate that the approach can accurately estimate queue lengths for an
approach lane at an intersection with a limited number of vehicles, which is an
essential consideration for traffic state estimation. Ultimately, the study's aims
are to apply the approach to estimating queue lengths in different scenarios and
provide a starting point for further research in traffic state estimation.  Additionally,
the method's applications extend to traffic state estimation to a range of scenarios
including left turns, right turns, and pedestrian flow. The study's approach can be
extended to estimating other relevant traffic stream properties in various contexts.

Nevertheless, current cross-domain models typically rely on substantial overlap between users from different domains, which can be a challenging requirement to meet in many cases. Furthermore, existing models fail to fully leverage the dual structure inherent to cross-domain recommendation tasks, overlooking bidirectional latent connections between users and items and resulting in suboptimal recommendation performance. To address these challenges, this study introduces a novel cross-domain recommendation framework based on Dual Learning, allowing information to be transferred iteratively between two domains until the learning process converges. Additionally, we propose a novel technique allowing users and items to learn shared latent factors across domains through a bidirectional mechanism. This model is then combined with a dual attention mechanism to adaptively aggregate information from other domains. Finally, a ranking score for each item is generated by aggregating the relevance from all connected domains. We evaluate the model on two large-scale industrial datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art baselines in terms of recommendation accuracy. Moreover, we show that our model's ability to find latent connections enables it to outperform other models in cross-domain scenarios with limited user overlap. This study further introduces a new benchmark dataset enabling recommender systems to handle cross-domain user groups of any size, enhancing the realism and feasibility of future research in this area. Through simulation studies, the estimators have been shown to enhance meta-analyst's power while remaining resilient against several sources of bias.  The proposed estimators are made available for public use through the R package metaAccrual version 1.0.0, accompanying the accompanying preprint, "Enhancing Power in Meta-analyses of Dependent Effect Sizes with Cluster-Robust Estimators".  Additionally, a companion software tutorial demonstrates the step-by-step process of implementing the estimators using real-world meta-analytic data..

considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In an effort to facilitate further NLP innovation, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. It is our hope that by addressing the negation challenge in NLP through CONDAQA will propel the development of more robust language models. The dataset is available at https://github.com/alan-jia

However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average distance between molecules. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within the scale of the Kolmogorov length. Specifically, the dissipation range is found to start at a length scale $\eta$ within the range of millimeters to centimeters, depending on the fluid viscosity and temperature. Since most laboratory turbulence experiments start with scales far beyond $\eta$, we conclude that turbulence is generally in a non-equilibrium, fluctuating state, regardless of whether it's caused by these small-scale fluctuations or other factors. This conclusion also applies to the study of magnetohydrodynamics, where similar comparisons are necessary for understanding the small-scale turbulence within astrophysical plasmas. Furthermore, we propose an experimental design for directly observing the dissipation range of turbulence in laboratory settings. This could provide valuable insights into the non-equilibrium states of turbulence in both classical fluids and plasmas. Such knowledge will help researchers determine whether the dissipation range is generally in a non-equilibrium, fluctuating state, or if it's affected by other factors. This study will greatly contribute to the development of future studies on magnetohydrodynamic turbulence.

Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent sound waves in an early universe. Gravity emerges from the radiation-induced Casimir effect.

This framework is based on an effective field theory that can also address the mass gap in Yang-Mills theories and is compatible with the holographic principle. Additionally, modifications to the Einstein field equations in a stationary spacetime setting are examined.

Lastly, the model predicts a minor deviation from the gamma-ray spectrum expected from a Dirac hole, indicating potential testing grounds. QL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can only handle queries based on knowledge that was learned during training. When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective beyond their training scope. Leveraging the success achieved in other areas of natural language processing, we developed an innovative approach that involves introducing a mechanism to copy elements directly from questions. By integrating this 'copy mechanism' into established Seq2Seq models like CNNs and Transformers, we can significantly boost their performance. We put this enhanced architecture to the test using state-of-the-art datasets containing questions that involve novel knowledge elements. Compared to their standard counterparts, our results indicate substantial improvements across all datasets. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the integration of the copy mechanism yields consistent gains over domain-specific handwriting-based approaches, even when those approaches are supplemented with additional training samples. Crucially, however, our results also highlight an important trade-off: while the copy mechanism offers superior performance, it also increases the query translation size by 15-20%. To address this concern, we developed an efficient 'thin-copy' method that removes unnecessary elements from the generated queries, resulting in no loss in accuracy while significantly reducing the query length. Interestingly, our findings suggest that the increased query length does not compromise its quality, as evaluated through the quality of resulting triples sets and the success rate of subsequent queries.

An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  An additional analysis considers various factors that influence whether a judge orders mental health treatment as part of probation and discovers it is more likely when the defendant is charged with a less violent crime, has no prior convictions, and the defendant's pre-sentence investigation recommends treatment, whereas judges are less likely to impose treatment when the defendant has prior convictions and is charged with more serious crimes.  An alternative treatment option could therefore involve providing financial support for probation officers to cover the costs of pre-sentence evaluations in an effort to enhance the efficacy of probation by increasing the use of mental health treatment. In contrast, the complete absence of credibility and certainty that a central bank will abandon its policies results in unstable inflation patterns. In the context of a standard New Keynesian Phillips curve model, the way the central bank adjusts policy tools in response to inflation discrepancies differs significantly between situations where a central bank can maintain its credibility and situations where it cannot. In addition to these differences, we find that the way a central bank adjusts policy tools in response to other shock variables may vary depending on whether a central bank maintains its credibility. In particular, when predicting larger than usual fluctuations in key economic variables, a non-collusive central bank tends to utilize larger adjustments in policy tools, including shorter-term interest rates and money supplies, whereas the effect of uncertainty regarding a central bank's policies on output-inflation adjustments is relatively minimal. Finally, in examining the effect of uncertainty regarding a central bank's policies on current policy tool adjustments, our research reveals two contrasting scenarios. Traditional relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum field theory can be derived from our theory by partitioning event Hilbert spaces into spatial and temporal components, and then focusing on temporal aspects. The local work function serves as evidence of structural, electronic, and chemical variations at surfaces, whereas Kelvin probe force microscopy enables the measurement of local contact potential differences, related to the work function. In this study, we employ this technique to chart the local contact potential differences of graphene nanoribbons grown on an Au(111) substrate. The local contact potential difference maps indicate a transfer of charge between the graphene nanoribbons and the gold substrate. Our findings are further validated through density functional theory calculations that demonstrate the maps accurately represent the doping of nanoribbons. Ultimately, these results contribute to an improved understanding of the relationship between atomic structures and electronic properties. By utilizing local contact potential difference mapping, we can investigate the charge transfer between different materials at the atomic level, facilitating the creation of nanoscale devices that take into account specific doping requirements. Furthermore, this approach provides a convenient means of monitoring real-time changes to the local work function during chemical reactions, thereby facilitating a deeper comprehension of action mechanisms at the atomic level. The technique has been successfully utilized to visualize distinct segments within a single nanoribbon, each with unique doping characteristics, as well as tribological effects on doping profiles. The method offers a valuable tool for studying local work functions, thereby enabling the extraction of valuable information about surface structures, electronic properties, and chemical compositions at the atomic level.

Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. This paper explores the diffusive transport of a Brownian particle moving through a narrow, conically-shaped channel under intermittent dynamics, namely stochastic resetting. This model averaging method has been complicated by differences between users, which causes global models to diverge and take longer to stabilize. Researchers introduced knowledge distillation as a potential solution by having the server refine its model with knowledge collected from diverse users, bypassing direct parameter averaging. Our new idea involves using data-free knowledge distillation to address heterogeneity in FL by having the server develop a simple generator to combine user information, and then distributing it to users to inform local training and boost generalization capabilities. Experimental results show that our method significantly improves generalization while using fewer communication steps compared to current top approaches. We also analyze the challenges and limitations of implementing our solution in real-world applications. This study provides insights on integrating our method with current FL systems, and we demonstrate the full code on an image classification task across various FL settings. We then explore its potential applications in settings with limited system resources and showcase its ability to deliver effective models with minimal communication. Ultimately, we observe that our method produces robust and generalizable models despite being simple and efficient. This study provides a foundation for further research on using server-generated knowledge to improve user local training in FL.

This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Recent breakthroughs in machine learning technology enable scientists to process data with higher precision and identify various quantum phases, even when contaminated with noise. We demonstrate the effective classification of topological phase transitions using a machine learning technique, specifically a deep convolutional neural network trained with noisy experimental data from a protected topological system of coupled fermions and spins. Applying this model to unseen data yielded a comprehensive phase diagram, with predicted phase transitions matching conventional findings on data with higher signal quality. Furthermore, analyzing the convolutional layer's filter and output responses reveals that the CNN relies on spin imbalance information to classify the phase transitions, but does so more efficiently in the presence of noisy data. Our findings indicate the promising potential of machine learning methods for various quantum systems. Future research will focus on training quantum states for more intricate models, such as the toric code, using a similar approach. Additionally, integrating the constraint of row or column closure into the CNN training process will enable the detection of closed manifold topological phases. We also anticipate that the most effective machine learning models will often exhibit interpretable results, allowing researchers to gain new insights into the characteristics of quantum phases. We make our code and data available to facilitate replication of our research and advancement of topological phase detection. See Supplemental Material below. [References] [Source]

Research on this complex phenomenon involves diverse spatial, temporal, and social contexts across the globe, with implications for socio-political dynamics throughout history. A crucial area of study within this field seeks to establish reliable predictors of gentrification and/or displacement, with a goal of developing proactive early warning systems. This research builds upon existing scholarship by investigating the essential methodological aspects needed to ensure that these systems can effectively prevent harm and promote justice. A key obstacle to overcome is identifying the right balance between generalizability and specificity when operationalizing concepts like "community" and "neighborhood change." Another critical challenge involves validating measures of gentrification and/or displacement that reflect the experiences of long-term resident communities. This research addresses these challenges by incorporating a community-based validation process of existing quantitative measures, adapting them to local contexts through social research. It also employs a multi-level logistic regression model to test its effectiveness as a predictive tool, while considering the inherent complexities of gentrification as a social phenomenon. An essential methodological requirement for any predictive model used in this context is that it should 1) be developed in partnership with the community that will be impacted, 2) be transparent in terms of its underlying assumptions and data sources, 3) be able to provide early warnings that enable residents to make informed decisions about their living situations, and 4) be able to differentiate between various forms of neighborhood change and/or displacement experiences. AR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. Measurements of plasma density and temperature showed the source can achieve optimal conditions rapidly after being modified. Furthermore, it was found that changing the reflectors in the plasma chamber had a profound impact on plasma density, and the source could achieve helicon mode at the facility's highest magnetic field with these modifications. Data from the IShTAR facility also verified the predictions of the plasma source model. Overall, it was determined that the plasma source can function effectively in helicon mode, and this capability is critical for the IShTAR facility to successfully investigate plasma interaction with radio frequency waves. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Additionally, the paper provides a manual prior incorporation strategy to incorporate pathologists' expertise into the model. Extensive experiments conducted on 5 publicly accessible datasets reveal that the proposed W-Net achieves competitive results and outperforms existing U-Net based models, particularly in terms of detecting small nuclei.

we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes the dominant source of electromagnetic and gravitational waves. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. We refer to these benchmark datasets as 'bright spots.' A discriminant analysis indicates that these bright spots contribute significantly to expertise differentiation within their respective domains. Clustering algorithms can be evaluated using either internal or external validation metrics. Internal validation metrics evaluate various aspects of partitioned data, but the clusterings they suggest may lack meaning. External validation metrics compare algorithm outputs to expert-provided reference groupings, employing metrics like normalised mutual information or adjusted Rand index. It is unclear whether incorporating semi-supervised learning is still beneficial when combined with a large-scale language model. This study aimed to resolve this uncertainty by comparing three data-to-text systems: one that solely utilizes a language model, and two systems enhanced with a data augmentation-based semi-supervised learning method, using either a small or a large language model for mixing, respectively.

Moreover, when comparing the two semi-supervised learning systems, the one using a large language model for mixing achieved higher scores in most metrics, despite initial expectations that a small model would be more effective due to potential language model contamination. Overall, the findings suggest that semi-supervised learning remains beneficial even when combined with a large language model and that such methods can enhance data-to-text generation performance. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. To tackle this optimization problem in the presence of channel state uncertainty and noise, a reinforcement learning solution inspired by the multi-armed bandit problem is proposed. Simulations show the new technique converges quickly in dynamic channel conditions and offers up to 75% better performance than conventional methods in terms of spectral efficiency. Additionally, the technique demonstrates up to 40% improved performance in terms of average data transfer rate when compared to traditional methods. Experimental results also validate the effectiveness of the proposed technique in real-world scenarios with varying levels of noise and channel conditions. The technique's efficiency comes at a processing cost of around 15.91 million instructions per second, making it suitable for implementation on modern embedded systems. We addressed this challenge through the use of strain engineering in ordered vertical stacks of SiGe quantum dot pairs. The lower dot in each pair creates favorable conditions for the upper dot to form by exerting strain that also stretches the silicon cap above. The confined electrons exhibit stronger overlap with the heavy holes near the upper dot's peak. Our approach involves embedding these dot pairs within complex structures like superlattices and wells, which allow for independent control of strain and composition. The impact of photonic stop-gaps on photoluminescence (PL) emission is also explored. A notable increase of nearly two orders of magnitude in PL intensity was observed when the emission wavelength is positioned within a photonic stop-gap, while red-shifted excitation laser energy led to a notable suppression of non-radiative recombination pathways. These findings indicate the efficacy of our design strategy for developing high-efficiency Si-based light emitters. The projected applications include efficient green laser sources and efficient light emitters for silicon photonic technologies. Our research provides a foundation for further investigation into the design of efficient Si-based light emitters. Our novel design of quantum dot pairs addresses long-standing challenges in achieving efficient light emission from Si/SiGe heterostructures by overcoming non-radiative recombination pathways through strain engineering and photonic confinement. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The study also provides insight into the movement of one screen, suggesting it travels in the direction of the Galactic rotation at approximately 13.5 km/s. To further understand scintillation patterns, it is recommended that future observations include measurements of the polarization angle of the pulsar. The analysis also recommends utilizing more sophisticated models that take into consideration various factors affecting scintillation, such as the changing position of the screens relative to the pulsar and the associated fluctuations in their properties. It sets a new benchmark for the emotion classification of social media posts containing text and images. The proposed method exhibits impressive performance even when the input data is partially annotated, showcasing its potential for real-world applications in social media emotion classification. Our research centers on single layer networks where binary synapses are used to learn random patterns, a statistical problem where solutions are predominantly isolated and extremely difficult to locate algorithmically.
In this work, we introduce a novel stochastic learning procedure which systematically explores the vast solution space to identify and stabilize such isolated solutions.
Our results show that with as few as two binary synaptic weights, the number of required neurons can be significantly reduced, from $N^2$ to $N\log(N)$, substantially reducing computational complexity.
Additionally, by employing multiple discrete synaptic states, the number of required neurons can be further minimized, yielding even larger reductions in computational complexity.
To illustrate the practical applications and benefits of these results, we show examples of enhancing neural controllers for robotic movements and simplifying classification tasks for image processing at reduced computational cost.

However, these tools face practical and theoretical limitations when it comes to dealing with complex objectives that are difficult to combine or reduce to one another. Philosophers have discovered a number of impossibility theorems stemming from this challenge, indicating that there may be no effective way to define what it means for an outcome to be beneficial without disregarding fundamental human ethics. As this problem has significant implications for high-stakes systems like AI medical decision support and autonomous weapons, these systems should refrain from using objective functions in a strict mathematical sense.

One potential solution is to utilize uncertain objectives, such as partially ordered preferences or probability distributions over total orders, instead of fixed objective functions. By exploring this alternative, it is possible to reinterpret previously established impossibility theorems as uncertainty theorems and derive lower bounds on the degree of uncertainty implied by these results. Ultimately, the relationship between objective uncertainty and unintended AI consequences remains a pressing question, prompting two key conjectures about the relationship between uncertainty and system malfunction. Research has emerged in analyzing fluid flow behavior based on single trajectory analysis: trajectory stretching exponent and trajectory angular velocity, which identify hyperbolic and elliptical behaviors respectively. This paper presents a critique of these methods in the expanded phase space and their lack of objectivity. This measure, called the trajectory vorticity, has been independently verified using two approaches: reducing flow instability and by considering the relative rotation of objects. Results show that the trajectory vorticity accurately detects rotation regardless of the trajectory distribution, outperforming the other methods, and further confirms the link between trajectory angular velocity and trajectory vorticity. The trajectory vorticity was also adapted for use in three-dimensional environments and demonstrated effective detection of rotation using fewer three-dimensional trajectories than two-dimensional trajectories. In addition, the paper presents formulas for calculating the trajectory vorticity in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system. The results show that a robotic system that follows this approach is capable of accurately navigating around obstacles in a familiar environment. This study also provides insights into the role of prior knowledge in such systems. The implemented system successfully navigates using the mental frameworks learned from similar tasks as prior knowledge. Moreover, this work reveals that active inference can be used to develop self-imposed constraints that facilitate safe and efficient navigation in unfamiliar environments. The implemented system demonstrates its ability to adapt to new environments by constraining its movement until it acquires more information about its surroundings. The experiments show that this approach leads to more efficient navigation compared to systems that do not utilize prior knowledge. The code and mental framework models used in this study are publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/openbrain

we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term are established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method are presented to validate the theoretical findings. Since deriving an optimal observability inequality for the structure-acoustic interaction model remains an unresolved issue within the current theoretical framework, numerical simulations are particularly crucial in determining the reasonable domain for the source term. Nonetheless, by leveraging the ability to precisely record boundary data from the structure and assuming a finite-dimensional representation of the source term, numerical results validate the theoretical stability estimate and confirm that the proposed method is feasible and reliable. Additionally, numerical experiments reveal that assuming a finite-dimensional source term allows for the resolution of source terms with fewer measurements than required by the theoretical stability estimate alone. Consequently, the theoretical framework and numerical results presented can facilitate the accurate determination of dense modes in the structure-acoustic interaction model. This method, inspired by Dyson-Schwinger and Bethe-Salpeter equations, represents nonperturbative kernels via contact interactions. By utilizing a novel subtraction scheme, we circumvented the standard procedures for handling divergent integrals that typically lead to symmetry breakdown. We specifically implemented the technique to investigate heavy-light mesons, focusing on the pseudoscalar pion and Kaon. We successfully solved the Dyson-Schwinger equation for the u, d, and s quark propagators and computed the bound-state Bethe-Salpeter amplitudes while satisfying the Ward-Green-Takahashi identities, which encapsulate the global symmetries of the model for any arbitrary momentum routing in the loop integrals. This technique allowed us to systematically approach the heavy-light mass spectrum while maintaining symmetry continuity. Our findings for the pion and Kaon masses agree with existing Dyson-Schwinger model results and experimentally observed values, respectively. Notably, our model correctly predicts a mass spectrum for the Kaon that increases with strangeness. This represents a significant achievement, as previous models that successfully predicted the pion masses often predicted a Kaon spectrum that decreases with strangeness. Our work now lays the groundwork for investigating phenomena involving light quarks in the presence of heavy quarks, such as deep inelastic scattering

Resource Allocation (ONRA) plays a vital role in service provisioning. As a sequential problem with uncertain outcomes, it presents a suitable case for tackling via Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, current RL solutions face significant challenges stemming from high sample complexity requirements. To navigate this hurdle, training RL agents in isolation is impractical due to a lack of knowledge about future service demands, while online training in actual networks causes performance deterioration due to temporary sub-optimal policies during prolonged learning periods. This degradation is particularly pronounced in non-stationary ONRA scenarios, where adapting to shifting service requirements is crucial. To circumvent this problem, a model-based resource allocation framework called RADAR is proposed, designed for ONRA applications with immediately known action effects. By strategically balancing exploration of the state space in the background with real-time policy exploitation, leveraging synthetic data generated from the trained environment model, RADAR effectively boosts sample efficiency. Additionally, RADAR empowers the development of follow-up strategies, enhancing its resource allocation decisions, after initial training has concluded. our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We also extend our analysis to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. In this case, our analysis yields a dual formulation that provides a more precise rate description, along with a manner in which this rate is consistently attained by random codes. DeepLATTE consists of a feature extractor module and a spatiotemporal learning module along with a semi-supervised learning strategy, which ensures that local and global correlation patterns of predictions match those found in observed data. A novel method called IntraStructural Data Augmentation (ISDA) generates new samples based on the semantically-rich relationships between classes and compounds, producing improved results with our proposed approach. Nevertheless, typical Graph Convolutional Networks rely on predefined skeletal connections and disregard dynamic interrelationships such as those between head, hand, and foot joints. Although effective in NLP and image description, the attention mechanism has been largely unexplored in current action recognition approaches. We propose a new spatial attention mechanism that adapts from a local to a global focus based on relative spatial metrics. Additionally, our design introduces a new initial graph adjacency matrix that connects distant skeletal joints like those in the head, hands, and feet. We evaluate the proposed model on two challenging, large-scale datasets: NTU-RGB+D and Kinetics skeleton, showing improved recognition performance across both benchmarks. Furthermore, our results reveal the efficacy of the designed adjacency matrix in focusing spatial attention on key interrelationships. Due to their comparable performance, our method is now more accessible and efficient than ever. The source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/ASAM.

Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the difficulty in defining attributes and preserving query uniqueness. Although fashion instance-level image retrieval and fashion attribute manipulation are crucial in real-world applications, most studies have focused on one problem alone. In this research, we aim to achieve state-of-the-art results on both tasks. To accomplish this, we propose a novel method that translates a query into a representation that incorporates the desired attributes. By introducing feature-level attribute manipulation, we match the manipulated features with real ones, allowing for independent attribute manipulation from the image representation. This breakthrough empowers existing image retrieval methods to perform attribute manipulation without compromising retrieval performance. Our approach demonstrates a notable performance boost over existing methods by achieving a record-breaking 60.8% accuracy in attribute manipulation and surpassing previous work with state-of-the-art performance in fashion instance-level image retrieval. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a listing of related papers. Currently, Daany is available for installation as a NuGet package, with plans to publish it in the Microsoft Open Source repository, as well as explore its potential for inclusion in the.NET Core distribution. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. This reinterpretation of Galileo's role in science aims to provide a fresh insight into the historical development of physics, as well as the intricate relationships between mathematics and science. This reevaluation also hopes to inspire young physicists by demonstrating that even those who excel in science can be deficient in mathematics, as long as they focus on their core strengths. Finally, it is suggested that Galileo's scientific legacy, which has historically been praised for its rigor and scientific methodology, was actually built upon his shortcomings in mathematics, as a result of his unique combination of scientific talents and personal limitations. This unusual reversal of fortune might encourage contemporary scientists to be more mindful of their own unique abilities and strengths

The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image with predefined offsets, making the process intricate and labor-intensive. This paper proposes a novel cost constructor, designed with convolutional neural networks, to efficiently generate matching cost for light field depth estimation. Our constructor, leveraging specifically engineered dilation rates, seamlessly combines pixels under predetermined disparities without any shifting, thereby ensuring a faster processing time. The proposed constructor also possesses occlusion-aware properties, enabling the dynamic modulation of pixels from different views and the effective handling of occlusions. By incorporating this innovative constructor, a deep learning-based light field depth estimation network has been developed, yielding the top results in the MSE category on the standard 4D LF benchmark, as well as outperforming other state-of-the-art approaches in terms of running speed. The proposed method has been found to be particularly effective under various complex scenes and conditions. The source code of our paper has been made publicly accessible at: https://github.com/SauerOfCourse/LF-Matching-Cost-Constructor. Additionally, the completed LFD network has been made available at: https://sauerofcourse.github.io/LF-Dense-DPS.html. The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. It is now part of the open-source library PySINDy and can be used directly. Additionally, we have developed a C++ implementation that can be integrated into existing codebases using the SINDy library.
